sections.h2: The Danville housing market for a seller
sections.html:
Danville is an affordable, slower-moving market where repair costs can rival a house's value. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $79,000. The city is the seat of Vermilion County, with 28,138 residents, down from 33,027 in 2010. Owner-occupied homes make up 57.3 percent of housing, median gross rent is $846, and there are 11,901 households of about 2.19 people.

Many Danville sellers are heirs, landlords with aging rentals, or owners of houses that have sat empty. When a roof or furnace costs a large share of what the house would sell for, an as-is sale deserves a serious look next to a listing.

If the house is empty, Danville's Chapter 169 can add registration fees that must be settled before the house changes hands. The owner of a vacant building must register with the Public Development Department within 30 days after the building becomes vacant.

Danville vacant building rules that matter at closing
RuleWhat the ordinance requires
Who must registerThe owner, within 30 days after the building becomes vacant
Residential registration fee$50 (non-residential is $100)
Annual fee if the building stays vacant$500, held in abeyance while permitted repairs make progress
Fees at transferPaid by the owner before any transfer, and disclosed by the seller to the buyer
If unpaid at transferNew owner pays the annual fee plus $300 within 30 days
Penalty for violations$250 to $2,500 per offense, with each day counted separately

A new owner must also re-register a vacant building within 30 days of any transfer and follow the plan the previous owner filed until changes are approved. A building counts as vacant when it is unoccupied and, for example, unsecured, unsafe, under an order to correct violations or illegally occupied. Ask the Public Development Department whether your property is on the registry before you sign a contract.

If the house is vacant and you plan to sell soon, a practical order is: confirm the registry status, pay any fee that is owed, get a payoff letter for any lender, and tell the buyer in writing about every fee on the property. A cash buyer will usually ask about this up front, and having the answer ready keeps the closing date from slipping. If repairs are underway under a permit, mention that too, since the annual fee is held in abeyance while permitted work makes progress.

Utility accounts and code enforcement are the two other places the city touches a sale. The utility billing office is at 17 W Main Street. Bring a signed and dated copy of the deed so the account can be prorated, because accounts are billed by date of ownership, not occupancy.

  • Account name: residential accounts must be in the owner's name, and a landlord's bill stays in the landlord's name.
  • Flat fees: every property owner pays flat sewer and solid waste fees regardless of usage, so a vacant house still gets a bill.
  • Due dates: accounts beginning with 08 are due on the 8th of each month and those beginning with 04 on the 20th, adjusted when the date falls on a weekend.
  • Rental registration: all rental units and vacant structures must be registered and a fee paid each year.

Common code violations include grass over six inches, trash in the yard, inoperable vehicles, missing house numbers and toters left out too long. Clearing those cheaply before showings makes the house look cared for and avoids a notice during the sale.

Deeds for Danville property go to the Vermilion County Recorder at 201 N Vermilion Street, Danville, Illinois 61832. The office phone is (217) 554-6040, and it accepts documents by mail if you include a check for the exact fee and a self-addressed return envelope.

Every sale or gift needs a newly prepared, signed, notarized and recorded deed. When the sale involves consideration above $100, Illinois Form PTAX-203 must be completed and submitted with the deed. The form collects the state and county transfer taxes, which are based on the sale price. A gift is exempt from those taxes, but the deed must carry the right exemption statement. The state rate, set in 35 ILCS 200/31-10, is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500.

Recorder staff cannot offer legal advice, run title searches or refer you to an attorney, so line those up yourself. A copy of a recorded deed costs $1.00 per page, and a deed presented in person is usually returned within five minutes of scanning. For current recording fees, call the office, because the schedule is revised from time to time. Questions about back taxes go to the County Treasurer, and parcel details to the Supervisor of Assessments.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited or estate house
sections.html: If the house came to you from an estate, ask an attorney whether title is clear before accepting any offer. Gather the recorded deed, the latest tax bill and the utility account details. Because every sale or gift needs a newly prepared deed, the names on the new deed must match the people who actually hold title. Buyers who pay cash generally still require clean title, so sort out any missing signatures before you pick a closing date.

sections.h2: Cash buyer or listing in Danville
sections.html:
Set the numbers side by side and include the costs that never appear in an offer. A house valued near the city median of $79,000 can leave little room for repairs, agent fees and months of carrying costs, so a quick as-is closing can be worth more than it first appears.

  • Get written repair bids for the roof, furnace, plumbing and electrical items an inspector would flag.
  • Check whether the building is registered as vacant and whether any fees are owed.
  • Ask for the closing date and confirm who pays recording and title charges.
  • Compare the figure against a listing agent's price opinion for the same house.

Illinois law requires you to deliver a residential disclosure report before the contract is signed under 765 ILCS 77/20, even when you sell as-is.

On closing day expect to sign the deed before a notary, sign the PTAX-203 declaration, and receive a settlement statement showing payoffs and prorated charges. Call the utility billing office with the deed copy the same week so the final bill is cut on the right date, and keep proof that any vacant building or rental registration fee was paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a vacant house in Danville?
faqs.a: Yes. If the house is registered as vacant, the city ordinance requires the fees to be paid before transfer and disclosed to the buyer. An unpaid annual fee passes to the new owner with an extra $300.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for a Danville sale?
faqs.a: Take or mail it to the Vermilion County Recorder at 201 N Vermilion Street in Danville. A sale above $100 also needs Illinois Form PTAX-203 filed with the deed.

faqs.q: How do I transfer utilities when my Danville house sells?
faqs.a: Bring a signed and dated copy of the deed to the utility billing office at 17 W Main Street or email it. The city prorates the account by date of ownership.

faqs.q: Do I owe a transfer tax to the city of Danville?
faqs.a: State and county transfer taxes are collected through the PTAX-203 form. Ask the title company to confirm the exact charges that apply to your sale.

faqs.q: Do I have to register my Danville rental before selling it?
faqs.a: Rental units must be registered and a fee paid each year. Contact the code enforcement office to confirm the registration is current before you sell.
